Q: How to run one thread at a time, ensuring previous one succeeds before moving on? A:

Just to be clear, you want to create 100 concurrent threads, and then have them each wait their turn before doing something. Is that right?

Of course there are many ways to solve that problem. The first one that comes to my mind is maybe not the mfost parsimonious with resources, but think it is elegant.

I would have the threads pass a "token" from one to the next, on down the line until every thread has held it. Each thread would wait to receive the token, then it would do the thing, and then it would hand the token off to the next thread in line. The token either could be a real object that is passed from thread to thread through blocking queues, or it could be a "virtual" token that is passed by signaling Semaphores. You'll need to create one queue or semaphore for each thread—probably in the same loop that creates the threads.

I'll leave it to you to figure out how to make sure that each thread gets a reference to the queue or semaphore that it waits on and, a reference to the one that it should wake when its task is done.

Q: Oracle 11g Maximum Processes/Sessions/Transactions limits A:

That's because you have probably hit your RAM limit or operating system limit. Each session created will reserve a certain amount of RAM, and sessions depends on processes.

From Oracle glossary, session is:

A logical entity in the database instance memory that represents the state of a current user login to a database. A single connection can have 0, 1, or more sessions established on it.

If shared server is ignored, you may well hit the limit of the PROCESSES parameter before you hit the limit of the SESSIONS parameter.

As a best practice, increase processes incrementally(like +200 or so), because if you increase it to a too high value, like you did, you will not be able to start your Oracle instance. Once you can't increase anymore, that 's your limit.
